books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text:
“I was once a tool of oppression,
And as green as a sucker could be,
And monopolies banded together
To beat a poor hayseed like me.
The railroads and old party bosses
Together did sweetly agree;
And they thought there would be little trouble
In working a hayseed like me.
But now I’ve roused up a little
And their greed and corruption I see,
And the ticket we vote next November
Will be made of hayseeds like me.”

(“The Hayseed,” Farmers’ Alliance song, sung in Kansas in 1890)
stimulus.source_note: “The Hayseed,” Farmers’ Alliance song of the 1890s, sung to the tune of “Save a Poor Sinner Like Me.” Public domain; wording checked against the Nebraska Folklore Pamphlet 18 transcript (Federal Writers’ Project, 1938) of the Farmers’ Alliance paper version.

stem: The song as a whole best shows that Farmers’ Alliance members believed which of the following?

options.text: Farmers should accept low prices and wait for better times
options.misconception: The singer says he has roused up and sees their greed, not that he will wait.

options.text: Only the federal courts could protect farmers from monopolies
options.misconception: The song points to voting, not to the courts.

options.text: Farmers should answer economic power with their own political movement
Farmers should leave the land and seek work in factories
options.misconception: The song ends with farmers voting their own ticket, not leaving their farms.

rationales.A: Rousing up and seeing corruption is the opposite of waiting quietly for better times.
rationales.B: No court appears in the song. The answer it gives is a ticket of hayseeds.
rationales.C: The singer moves from being beaten to voting a ticket made of hayseeds like himself.
rationales.D: The song keeps the farmer on the land and sends him to the polls, not to a factory.
rationales.general:
Follow the singer’s change of mind.
1. At first the singer was a tool of oppression, beaten by monopolies.
2. Then he roused up and saw their greed and corruption.
3. The last lines turn that anger into a ticket voted next November.
4. Economic power, the song says, must be met with farmers’ own political power.
Remember: a protest song that ends at the ballot box is a call to organize.
